blocks.text: Such as the crested dove, common in India, which HASSELQUIST describes as entirely snow-white, Travels p. 333. The same author has this on the dove of Palestine, p. 553: “The size of a wood pigeon. The neck, head, breast and shoulders are grey. The back grey with dark spots. The tail feathers and flight feathers white at the tip. The eyes and feet are reddish.”

But Michaelis, in Supplemm. ad Lexx. vol. III, p. 950, note, rightly pointed out that this etymology is far too broad, since absolutely all metals are dug out of the earth. He nevertheless omitted what A. Schultens discussed concerning this word in Commentar. ad Prov. XXI, 5, p. 252. Gold seems to have been called חרוץ because in some places of Arabia Felix, where rain pours heavily over ground rich in gold, the gold is laid bare and so is found as if already dug out, not by art but of its own accord. See the passage from Taurizius, the grammarian, cited by Schultens in the place mentioned.
1 Par. XVI, 32. Ps. XCVI, 11. et XCVIII, 7. etc.

The ancient interpreters also understood the word מלאת, with unanimous agreement, of the fullness of waters, as Bochart explained above. See HUFNAGEL's [II, 539] Observationes in Canticum Canticorum (under the title Auch etwas übers hohe Lied) in the Repertorium für bibl. und morgenl. Litterat. edited by Eichhorn, vol. XI, p. 131. Moreover, what Bochart remarks here about the interpretation of the word מלאת devised by some of the Hebrews applies also to Velthusen, who in his commentary on this passage (Der Schwesternhandel, eine morgenländische Idyllenkette, mit historischkritischen Untersuchungen pp. 425–428) brings forward much from his manifold store of learning to explain the simile used by the Hebrew poet, but little, I suspect, that bears on the matter. By doves washed in milk our poet undoubtedly meant to express the pure and, as it were, radiant whiteness of the eyes around the pupils. That these doves are pictured as sitting by the waters belongs to the ornament of the image; no further simile should be sought in this. It is tedious to report the guesses of other interpreters.

The original sense of the verb הגה, which lies in seething heat, and the series of meanings derived from it, since it is then transferred to all the more agitated and vehement emotions, whether these seethe inwardly in the mind (hence it is also used of meditation, which for an Oriental is a kind of agitation and commotion of the mind) or boil over and burst out into murmurs, moaning, howls, cries (hence also of the roaring of a lion), and into songs, both mournful and satirical: all this ALB. Schultens uncovered and expounded with the help of the Arabic هجى [hajā] in his Commentarius in Prov. p. 320 ff., compare p. 71; further in his Commentar. in Iob. p. 1040, and in the Animadverss. Philologg. in Thren. Ierem. Chapter III, v. 62, p. 509.

But everything is plain, and there is no need either to supply some verb or to alter the received reading, if the verb נהג is explained from the Arabic نهج [nahaja] to sigh, to moan, to draw sighs, as ALB. Schultens first showed in Animadverss. Philoll. ad Nah. II, 7, p. 342; to whom add I. D. Michaelis in Supplemm. ad Lexx. Hebrr. vol. V, p. 1603.

Compare ALB. Schultens, Animadverss. Philologg. on Esaj. XIX. 17., p. 265 of the Opera minora, Leiden 1769. ED. Pococke shows a similar use of the Arabic verb فزع [fazaʿa] in his Commentar. on Hos. III, 5.

On carrier doves, whose service the Turks still use today for carrying letters, much is reported by DELLA VALLE in his Travels vol. I, letter 12, pp. 128–129 of the German translation (who asserts that a six days' journey is completed by a carrier dove in a single day), and by ALEX. RUSSELL in the Natural History of Aleppo p. 66. The plan of our work does not allow us to transcribe these passages here, since they are too long.
